messages.subject: Model parameters change with “predicting” data
parts:
Dear INLA experts,

I have noticed that the parameters of my GLMM slightly change in value depending on whether I fit the model only to the observational data or if I include “testing” or “predicting” data points (i.e., the points of my regular grid). Here is what I mean:

I fit my model like this:

-----------------------------------

MODS <- inla(formula = as.formula(FMLAS), data = hydrodata, family = "tweedie",
          control.family = list(hyper =  list(
              theta1 = list(initial = 1.725),
              theta2 = list(initial = -4,
                    prior = "loggamma",
                    param = c(100, 100)))),
             inla.mode = "experimental",
             num.threads = NC,
             verbose = T)

-----------------------------------

where “hydrodata” contains only observations and my model FMLAS is:

-----------------------------------

> FMLAS
[1] "CPUE ~ BATH + log(BATHGRAD):log(sumEP+1) + I(log(BATHGRAD)^2) + TEMP:log(sumEP+1) + I(TEMP^2):log(sumEP+1) + log(sumEP+1) + LON + LAT + I(LON^2) + I(LAT^2)"

-----------------------------------

After fitting, the model parameters are:

-----------------------------------

Dispersion parameter for Tweedie 39.69 0.456      38.80    39.68      40.59

-----------------------------------

Here are my questions:

1) Why do the model parameter values change with the “predicting” data? For me this makes no sense, since a prediction should be independent of the data used to train the model... Is this dependence of model parameters on the predicting data with INLA correct at all or I am doing or understanding something wrong? In case this is correct, is this some kind of “Bayesian” standard issue, i.e., kind of a concept which does not exist in frequentist statistics?

2) I wonder if it is at all needed to involve the predicting points in the INLA fitting procedure. Why not simply to make a prediction by fitting the model only to the observations and, once the model parameters have been found, *evaluating* the GLM in the predicting points?

Example of what I mean:

-----------------------------------

# Extract the model parameter values:
modparam <- MODS$summary.fixed$mean

# We need now to calculate the “model matrix”, but first,
# we need to indicate R to include NAs in the predictors to obtain
# also Nas in the model matrix (otherwise the model matrix is shorter
# in the missing values):
options(na.action='na.pass')

# Now here comes the model matrix, i.e., a matrix including a column per model
# term (including a column of 1s for the intercept) and each row being the
# model term evaluated in a testing point of “climdata”:
X0 <- model.matrix(as.formula(FMLAS), data = climdata)

# We have to mutiply now the model matrix X0 with the vector of model
# parameter values “modparam” *columnwise*. To do so, we define a
# matrix with the values of modparam in the diagonal and use the
# matrix multiplication operator %*% :
AB_ <- X0 %*% diag(modparam)

# Finally, we add the multiplication AB_ of fitted model
# parameters and model terms evaluated on the testing points and apply
# the inverse link function (in my case, it is a log link):
AB <- exp(as.vector(rowSums(AB_)))

-----------------------------------

Now we have the predicted response stored the variable AB, evaluated on a regular grid. This procedure is identical to what you obtain with the function gam() of mgcv and the function predict(). You can even compute error estimates for the response variable by using the 0.95 credible intervals instead of using the parameter means, i.e. repeat the procedure with:

-----------------------------------
modparam_high <- MODS$summary.fixed$"0.975quant"

modparam_low <- MODS$summary.fixed$"0.025quant"
-----------------------------------

So, why not to use this “evaluation” procedure instead of including the predicting points in the call to inla()? Does it have any disadvantage in comparison? Is this only possible in the absence of random effects? Otherwise:

How to do the “evaluation” procedure when you have random effects? I guess that you can extract the random parameters with MODS$summary.random but: is there also an equivalent “model matrix” for random effects? How to compute it?

I would guess you run in inla.mode="classic". I would suggest to upgrade
the R-INLA package to the most recent version (with R-4.2).

the new internal representation should be more consistent when expanding
the model (well, its all numerical issues...)

parts:
Thanks for answer, Håvard!

I am actually using "inla.mode = "experimental"" (see my MODS <- inla(...) above), that was the only way to get inla() to work with my large amount of data, otherwise the run froze (especially when I included testing points in the fit). The R version I'm using is 4.2.2, i.e., the newest as far as I know. But I don't really have to dig much into the issue, it is enough for me to know that the model parameters should (in theory) not change in value and that this is simply due to some numerical issue.

However, I would still like to have answer to my question #2... :-) Why do we need to involve the testing points in the "fitting" procedure? To use only the training data is considerably faster and after the model is fitted we can simply "evaluate" it on the desired testing points. I am only unsure if this is also possible when the model includes a random effect, since I do not know how to extract the parameters of the random effect or how to construct the corresponding model matrix to evaluate the model, but from my understanding of the theory, this should be possible for any GLMM, with no disadvantage at all.

> Here are my questions:
>
> 1) Why do the model parameter values change with the “predicting”
> data? For me this makes no sense, since a prediction should be
> independent of the data used to train the model... Is this dependence
> of model parameters on the predicting data with INLA correct at all or
> I am doing or understanding something wrong? In case this is correct,
> is this some kind of “Bayesian” standard issue, i.e., kind of a
> concept which does not exist in frequentist statistics?
>
> 2) I wonder if it is at all needed to involve the predicting points in
> the INLA fitting procedure. Why not simply to make a prediction by
> fitting the model only to the observations and, once the model
> parameters have been found, *evaluating* the GLM in the predicting
> points?
>
> Example of what I mean:
>
> -----------------------------------
>
> # Extract the model parameter values:
> modparam <- MODS$summary.fixed$mean
>
> # We need now to calculate the “model matrix”, but first,
> # we need to indicate R to include NAs in the predictors to obtain
> # also Nas in the model matrix (otherwise the model matrix is shorter
> # in the missing values):
> options(na.action='na.pass')
>
> # Now here comes the model matrix, i.e., a matrix including a column
> per model
> # term (including a column of 1s for the intercept) and each row being
> the
> # model term evaluated in a testing point of “climdata”:
> X0 <- model.matrix(as.formula(FMLAS), data = climdata)
>
> # We have to mutiply now the model matrix X0 with the vector of model
> # parameter values “modparam” *columnwise*. To do so, we define a
> # matrix with the values of modparam in the diagonal and use the
> # matrix multiplication operator %*% :
> AB_ <- X0 %*% diag(modparam)
>
> # Finally, we add the multiplication AB_ of fitted model
> # parameters and model terms evaluated on the testing points and apply
> # the inverse link function (in my case, it is a log link):
> AB <- exp(as.vector(rowSums(AB_)))
>
> -----------------------------------
>
> Now we have the predicted response stored the variable AB, evaluated
> on a regular grid. This procedure is identical to what you obtain with
> the function gam() of mgcv and the function predict(). You can even
> compute error estimates for the response variable by using the 0.95
> credible intervals instead of using the parameter means, i.e. repeat
> the procedure with:
>
> -----------------------------------
> modparam_high <- MODS$summary.fixed$"0.975quant"
>
> modparam_low <- MODS$summary.fixed$"0.025quant"
> -----------------------------------
>
> So, why not to use this “evaluation” procedure instead of including
> the predicting points in the call to inla()? Does it have any
> disadvantage in comparison? Is this only possible in the absence of
> random effects? Otherwise:
>
> How to do the “evaluation” procedure when you have random effects? I
> guess that you can extract the random parameters with
> MODS$summary.random but: is there also an equivalent “model matrix”
> for random effects? How to compute it?

> However, I would still like to have answer to my question #2... :-)
> Why do we need to involve the testing points in the "fitting"
> procedure? To use only the training data is considerably faster and
> after the model is fitted we can simply "evaluate" it on the desired
> testing points. I am only unsure if this is also possible when the
> model includes a random effect, since I do not know how to extract the
> parameters of the random effect or how to construct the corresponding
> model matrix to evaluate the model, but from my understanding of the
> theory, this should be possible for any GLMM, with no disadvantage at
> all.

this is how its implemented. you can always build predictions yourself
using inla.posterior.sample and eval(), see the vignette.

Ok, thanks, Håvard, it's great to know that I was on the right path then. This clarifies my second question. I would only kindly suggest to modify the documentation relating predictions with INLA, e.g.:

https://www.r-inla.org/faq#h.821k2r53fvx3

This, which is similar (identical?) to the section of the same name in the vignette "Short tutorials" (http://127.0.0.1:30577/session/Rvig.64e1c717c9dd8.html obtained with browseVignettes(package="INLA") in the R prompt), focuses on predictions being done "as a part of the model fitting itself", i.e., by appending the predicting points at the end of the training data frame. Taking a quick look to the other vignettes (which I did not know), I guess that your answer refers to "5.2 Cheaper way: Monte Carlo samples" (i.e., inla.posterior.sample) & "5.3 Prediction on a grid, cheaper way" (i.e., eval()?) of the SPDEhowto.pdf in the vignettes. Perhaps it would be good to cross reference those sections in the online FAQs (they are the first thing to pop up in a google search) or include a comment saying that the same can be done quicker by "evaluating" the fitted model.

All the best, Ismael.
